Two practitioners address their participation in an online discussion concerning psychoanalysis and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. One speaks from the perspective of a Palestinian-American and the other as a Jewish-Australian. They address several personal questions including why they joined the discussion, what was it like to be in it, how they came to work together, and who they are to each other as Palestinian and Jew. Larger questions are also posed: Where do psychoanalysis and politics meet? What is to be made of family trauma in public space? Where do loss and mourning come in? What can mutual recognition achieve applied to large, political contexts?

Mark Cohen

Mark Cohen

Mark Cohen   About the Author Mark Cohen works as a Consultant Psychotherapist within the NHS in Scotland. amark.cohen@ggc.scot.nhs.uk
bureaucracy, neoliberalism, ego ideal, perversion

This paper examines the undermining of formal processes and their necessary supporting structures in the light of the psychoanalytic theories of Chasseguet-Smirgel, in particular her use of the concepts of the ego ideal and perversion. It is argued that, in a perverse process, formal structures and procedures may be undermined, bypassed or dismantled. The author suggests that this is common in the contemporary culture of organisational life and is underpinned by neoliberal ideology. This argument is considered with reference to the work of the sociologist Paul du Gay, which focuses upon bureaucracy and a reading of the ideas of Max Weber. The impact of perverse processes on public bureaux in the UK is explored.

The genius of Todd McGowan’s new book, Enjoying What We Don’t Have: The Political Project of Psychoanalysis, is its astute simplicity. Very few are able to relate the complicated concepts of Lacanian and Freudian psychoanalysis without obfuscating their meaning; McGowan is not only able to do this, but accomplishes it with examples from Hamlet to The Da Vinci Code. Positing the Freudian death drive as the structural alternative to a traditional political program, McGowan offers a take on psychoanalytic politics that stands as a clear voice amidst the diverse Lacanian field. While previous cultural theorists such as Theodor Adorno read Freud for his work on the pleasure principle and sexual liberation, today’s Lacanian left focuses instead on Freud’s radicalization of the death drive and rejects the idea of reform within the existing system. The crucial difference here is that the psychoanalytic project does not aim to “change the world”, and that the usefulness of this project comes from its very lack of political dogmatism. If, in the clinical setting, the psychoanalytic cure does not aim to radically change the life of the subject but simply make her realize that “she is that”, then one could say that this particular politics is more a recognition of how society is constituted than a transformation of society itself. The fundamental aspect of this constitution is, of course, antagonism. While previous models of psychoanalytic politics maintained that society could eliminate this fundamental antagonism within the social order, the political project founded on the death drive finds this to be impossible.

The death drive, in McGowan’s words, arises from “a death that occurs within life”, rather than the death that occurs at the end of life (p. 35). It is an impulse to return to a traumatic loss of an object that creates the desiring subject. As subjects, we repeatedly return to the experience of this loss, which structures our enjoyment. Any attempt at the production of an object to fill this void never delivers the pleasure it promises, because it deprives the object of its very quality of desire. The goal for the subject of this project is to embrace loss and accept the idea that there is no object that can satisfy desire. This radical ethical relation translates to a political one by positing traumatic loss as the crux of politics, and reveals that the death drive is the mode by which the subject can reject the social authority’s attempts to provide it with solutions to fill the lack at both an individual and social level. Stephen Frosh  

The work of Jean Laplanche, who died on Freud’s birthday in 2012, has become well known across the English-speaking psychoanalytic world in the last decade or so, not least because of the efforts of John Fletcher and Nicholas Ray, who have both translated important Laplanchian texts from the French and also presented their own Laplanche-inflected scholarly work. Fletcher, for instance, has recently brought out a major single-authored book of his own, Freud and the Scene of Trauma (New York: Fordham, 2013), which develops several lines of thought inherited from Laplanche in order to reinstate the Freudian ‘seduction theory’. In that book, Fletcher carefully pares away Freud’s writings from first to last in order to show how seduction and the traumatic origin of sexuality continually return, even well after their famous repudiation in the late 1890s. This idea, that what we are faced with in Freudian theory is a tumultuous discovery that is denied or repressed but never lost, is one of the key ways in which Laplanche shakes up psychoanalytic orthodoxy; gradually, as more texts have appeared and more thoughtful commentaries have been written, it has become clear that this recovery of ‘seduction’ is not an aberration or weird piece of pornographic imagination, nor a peculiar, Masson-like climbing on an abuse train, nor even a sanctification of trauma to match the current ‘trauma culture’. Rather, it is a provocative but serious piece of reading and interpreting, an act of theoretical recovery that uncovers the traces that remain of the Freudian revolution; which is to say, it is a deeply psychoanalytic reading of psychoanalysis itself.

Seductions and Enigmas begins with this question of reading and interpretation, in an introduction by the editors that would be worth the price of the book on its own. For those not familiar with Laplanche, they offer a brief contextualising history, listing his main publications and noting the continuing fame and importance of the co-authored (with J-B. Pontalis) Language of Psychoanalysis (published in French in 1967 and then in English by the Hogarth Press in 1973) – still the best and most influential ‘dictionary’ of Freudian ideas. obsessional neurosis, Lacanian psychoanalysis, radical political philosophy, Slavoj Žižek, Alain Badiou

Obsessional politics gives name to what remains unsaid and under-examined within the contemporary political situation. If obsessional politics may be taken to refer to those tendencies within the political field whose symptomatic condition concerns a demand for novelty, and an avoidance of the goal of authentic novelty via the aim of repetition, it may be further assumed that obsessional politics operates according to the trinity of the obsessional neurotic: self-mastery, repetition, and novelty. Taken together, these three rings form the knot of obsessional politics. This article sets out to demonstrate that it is possible to form a post-obsessional knot by way of Jacques Lacan’s concept of “style,” Slavoj Žižek’s “act,” and Alain Badiou’s “event.”

This paper explores several paradigmatic approaches to understanding the causes of the intractability of the Israeli/Palestinian conflict. It elaborates a perspective that illuminates how the traumatic histories of both peoples construct a victim state of mind, whose paranoid schizoid mechanisms are exacerbated by the ongoing traumatogenic environment of violence and war, thus foreclosing capacities for peacemaking. After critiquing the trauma paradigm’s assumptions of psychological symmetry and shared responsibility for the conflict, the paper develops an alternative social psychoanalytic model that situates the unconscious processes produced by trauma within the specificities of history, large group identity, ideological hegemony and power hierarchies that shape the psychological experience of both peoples and account for the complex systemic asymmetries that impede the possibilities for a just reconciliation of their tragic conflict.

death, children, parents, grief, possession, identity

This essay examines the psychological, cultural and political consequences facing parents whose children have been victims of death from illness, suicide, drug addiction and murder. The narratives were taken primarily from participants in a local Compassionate Friends [grief] group. Questions explored include: what is the response of the cultural surround to parents who lose their children? How does the Compassionate Friends group function as a holding environment? How can we think about the power of grief overtaking the self and annihilating identity? And what is the impact on identity of a self shattered by this experience? Connections are drawn between the non-Western phenomenon of spirit possession and the phenomenology of possession by grief (and madness) in parents who have suffered this terrible tragedy. Buddhist approaches to dealing with the death of a child are contrasted with the horrifying and disintegrating grief that is so powerful in parents who have suffered the very difficult task of finding their way back to meaningful engagement with others.

Derek Hook

USA

Derek Hook  

Alain Badiou and Élisabeth Roudinesco Translated by Jason E. Smith, Columbia University Press, New York, 2014, 82 pp., $19.95 paper, ISBN: 978-0-231 165112

The recently published dialogues between French intellectuals Alan Badiou and Élisabeth Roudinesco make for fascinating reading, particularly when they consider the relationship between Lacan and psychology. The message here is clear-cut: from the perspective of Lacanian theory and practice, psychology is the enemy. As Roudinesco notes, “Lacan never stopped criticizing psychology as a false science” (pp. 10–11).

He opposed every form of identitarian closure that denies the alterity that constitutes us and he opposed the behaviourism and cognitivism that have reduced man to his naturality, reduced him to his biological being, to his body and his brain. (pp. 28–29)

When Roudinesco asks, “Are psychoanalysts destined to become psychologists…?” one cannot help but wonder what exactly she has in mind by “psychologists”. Her answer, with its obvious echo of Michel Foucault, is not long in coming: psychologists are “technicians of the soul” (p. 66). Understood in this way, psychology is both naively positivistic (a form of scientism), and necessarily tied to the objectives of a type of disciplinary normalization whereby – staying with Foucault – subjects must be assimilated into the contemporary judgments and values of society. A threefold attack on the various forms of psychology’s alleged reductionism (the respective reductionisms of behaviourism, cognitivism, and latterly, of neurology and neuroscience) is thus extended by means of a political assault which considers “psychologism” a “blatant ideological program” (p. 30).

The terms of this rejection of psychology are thrown into sharper relief when Roudinesco responds to a prompt by her interviewer, Christine Goémé:

C.G.: Isn’t one of the most important aspects of the Lacanian enterprise the fact that it stands in the way of any and all psychologization of the subject?

Philosophy and working-through the past: A psychoanalytic approach to social pathologies

Stefan Bird-Pollan

Stefan Bird-Pollan

USA

Stefan Bird-Pollan  

Jeffrey Jackson Lexington Books, Lanham, MD, 2013, 188pp., $80.00, ISBN-13: 978-0739182840

Jackson’s stimulating and important book will be of interest to psychoanalysts, cultural theorists and philosophers. It adds significantly to the already provocative Freudian theory that culture is a compromise formation between sexuality and aggression by showing that the basic structure of this dialectic is manic-depression, which Jackson analyzes as a defense against loss. Culture, in its manic-depressive form, is the rejection of separation, while culture in its mournful form is conceived as working-through, that is, the struggle to acknowledge separateness and hence also the self’s authority over its own destiny. This approach raises a number of important questions for psychoanalysis and social and political philosophy more generally, which I will explore after outlining Jackson’s main claims.

In pursuing his general thesis, Jackson makes three important contributions to the understanding of modern culture from a psychoanalytic point of view. The first is to show that Freud’s metapsychology, generally understood to be a neutral structure from which pathologies deviate, is itself essentially a diagnosis of a pathological reaction to loss, which Jackson terms a manic-depressive response. His second point is to show that the philosophical idea of a pure or transcendental ego (as in Kant and Husserl, for example), far from being a neutral structure akin to metapsychology, is also a defense against loss and originates in the same manic-depressive culture. Finally, Jackson addresses the possibility of overcoming manic-depressive culture through what he understands to be Freud’s (and Adorno’s) conceptions of working through the past, that is, acknowledging the relation of separation between self and other.

The key elements of Jackson’s reading of Freud’s metapsychology are given in chapter 1 and at the beginning of chapter 2. These two chapters are particularly fascinating for anyone interested in psychoanalytic cultural criticism and how it relates to metapsychology. Jackson presents his reconstruction in an object relations context, a theoretical setting congenial to the German philosophical heritage in which he wishes to situate Freud.

Philosophy of dreams

Oliver Decker

Oliver Decker

Germany

Oliver Decker  

Christoph Türcke, Susan H. Gillespie (Trans.), Yale University Press, 2013, 304 pp., $30.00, ISBN: 978-0300188400

Christoph Türcke, one of Germany’s leading contemporary intellectuals, is well known for his work in philosophy and the theory of religion, as well as for his presence in interdisciplinary academic and public discourse. In recent years, his publications have enjoyed broad attention from the media and academics alike.

Philosophy of Dreams is written from the perspective of a philosopher and scientist of religion who knows his psychoanalytic theory as well. In this study, Türcke develops what he calls a “mental archaeology” in which he attempts to reconstruct both the historical process of civilization and the process of imagination. In other words, he endeavors to understand the genesis of culture as well as the genesis of the mind. Türcke’s project is to grasp what makes our “iconic age” so necessary: his starting point is the description of the omnipresence of pictures, movies and images and their connection with computers, smart-phones and other enhancements. These tools mediate modern life, and in order to understand how and why contemporary life has evolved in this manner, Türcke goes back to the prehistory of our modernity. In arguing that high technologies lead straight back to the “Paleolithic age” – at least as far as the structure of the human mind is concerned – Türcke’s thesis is that both civilization and mental processes are results of a “traumatic compulsion to repeat”.

According to Türcke, the earliest history of humans is still present; it is concealed underground in the depths of the human mind, where prehistory and our earliest history are deposited or “sedimented”. But how can we understand the prehistory that might enable us to analyze the present? In this context, Türcke borrows a concept from Derrida to speak of a process of “de-sedimentation” brought about by the rhythms of the Industrial Revolution, during which the repetitive operations of industrial machinery began to dredge the lowest stratum of the human mind. The term “industry 2.0” gives an indication of the close conjunction between the early stages of industrialization and the recent era of digitalization. High technology products such as computers, smart-phones and television have given the repetition of industrial machines a new quality, the omnipresence of which dredges up the sediment that has accumulated in the course of human development.

Night garden

Dawn Skorczewski

Dawn Skorczewski

USA

Dawn Skorczewski  

326 Judith Harris Tiger Bark Press, Rochester, New York, 2013, 102 pp., $16.95 paper, ISBN-13: 978-0981675282

Judith Harris’s most recent volume of poetry, Night Garden, represents her most exquisite and lyrical work on human suffering, the reality of mortality, and the desiring subject. Divided into four sections, the volume is framed by an initial “Poem,” which names “patience for the intolerable” as “the hard part.” When patience moves, “like a funneling wind/shrieking right through the window panes,” it sears through us, but the speaker acts as guide, juxtaposing images of fecundity and growth with those that speak immanent death. She is “a vase in the shape of a woman/with lillies pending from her mouth,” but also “meticulously glued together,/crack upon crack.”

If Harris offers a cracked poetic subject, she also cracks open her world for us. In “Root,” father and mother stand at the front of their house, where “nothing changes.” This couple cannot help their daughter, who looks for meaning even as they ritualistically shut it down all around her. In “My Mother Folding Linens,” the meticulous laundress closes the door “on what will keep.” One imagines that the daughter lives in that closed place with the laundry, keeping silent until she can speak her truth. “Neighborhood” finds her with mother’s umbrella, strolling out with it while “sucking on lemons.”

Just when the bitter taste of stasis feels like it could become too much, Harris lands us firmly in the light. In “Light’s Portrait,” we learn that “white feather and ash bone,/from above the world is never separate.” The lesson becomes one of height and depth, of connection through and even with pain. In “Night Garden,” we discover the resilience: “some flowers/won’t dissolve into the darkness.” Utilizing Lacan’s description of the mirror, imaginary, and symbolic stages, the speaker tries to sift out this human and narcissistic need for spectral identification, rather than casting off the unseen flowers into the flux and meaninglessness: “This world is a mirror glass/how is it we find images/of ourselves in places/we can’t bear to see.” A confrontation with the true emptiness of death as irrefutable would be intolerable and unbearable. Instead we supply the image as a mirage, a necessary illusion.

Respect, plurality, and prejudice: A psychoanalytical and philosophical enquiry into the dynamics of social exclusion and discrimination

Edward Weisband

Edward Weisband

USA

Edward Weisband  

Lene Auestad Karnac Books, London, 2015, 310 pp., $53.95 paper, ISBN-13: 978-1-782-20139-7

Prejudice, discrimination and varied forms of social exclusion exact immeasurable human cost and suffering seemingly everywhere in the modern world. The broad manifestation of prejudice adheres to categorical reifications congealed around fixed, fixated, and substantialist forms of contempt as witnessed across many cultures. But essentialist categories arise and gain traction in ways calibrated to the specific power formations and social dynamics of any national society and traditional community. The consequences include social subordination, political domination and economic exploitation, but these too operate differently within contrasting historical formations. Discriminatory practices, exclusivist doctrines, and forms of prejudicial justification are thus universally similar but culturally different in their origins, causes and reinforcements.

Categorical assumptions embedded within prejudicial or exclusivist social or communal value systems foment particular kinds of effects including political extremism, xenophobia, majority nationalism, ethno-centrism, paternalism, classism, racism, kinship, blood or tribal nativism, caste honor exclusivism, clientism, anti-Semitism, homophobia, sexism, misogynist or gender essentialism, ageism, and ableism, etc. How and why cultural mores and predispositions do so differ from place to place and in ways that reveal intergenerational influences that speak to time and continuity and thus to collective ways of life. Such ways of life, grounded by inter-subjective meanings and patterns of social interaction, reflect material distributions of social, economic and political power, as well as concrete and cognized value structures. But they also reveal the embedded but elusive crustaceans of unconscious and/or preconscious prejudice – so often expressed non-verbally, but conveyed viscerally or implicitly, and all the more powerful in their hurtful impacts as a result. Thus the practical methods of prejudice and how they function in influencing human behaviors are not only concrete and material. They operate as cognitive and ideological formations that in turn take hold in constellations of psychic and emotional beliefs and attitudes as well as in the subterranean casts of unconscious predispositions or preconscious proclivities that are themselves the results of socio-economic, political and, in particular, cultural history.

Roger Kneebone  

simulation, fantasy, technology, virtual reality, work, medical education

Medicine is increasingly taught in immersive simulated environments to supplement the apprenticeship model of work-based learning. Clinical research on this educational practice focuses on its realism, defined as a property of simulation technology. We treat realism as a function of subjective but collectively organized perception and imbued with fantasy, which we define by drawing on Lacanian studies of virtual reality and workplace organization. Data from an observational study of four simulation centres in London teaching hospitals is drawn on to present an account of what was taught and learned about medicine, including medical failure, when medical practice was simulated.

Uri Hadar

Israel

Uri Hadar   About the Author Uri Hadar is Professor of psychology at Tel Aviv University. His research interests include the neural substrates of language processing, the uses of hand gestures, Lacanian psychoanalysis and the post-colonial analysis of the Israeli occupation. His book Psychoanalysis and Social Involvement has recently been published by Palgrave MacMillan.

resistance, subject, part object, oppression, repression, Israel, Palestine

Social and political oppression of a designated social group may be compared to repression in the individual domain. In both cases, there is an agency that acts as an oppressor or repressor, which agency arouses resistance in the oppressed. Resistance aims to liberate the oppressed/repressed from the subjugating agency. The question that I address in the present paper is whether there is any advantage in resisting oppression or repression jointly with the oppressor or the repressor. Such advantage may emerge if we deconstruct the separateness between the oppressor and the oppressed-repressor and repressed. Such a deconstruction gives rise to more hybrid notions of power relations. My paper examines these issues in two distinct domains: that of psychoanalysis (with special reference to therapy) and post-colonial theory (with special reference to the Israeli Occupation in the West Bank and Gaza). The results of my deconstruction are formulated in terms derived from the work of Melanie Klein, especially the concept of ‘part object’. I freely extend this term to refer to forms of partial subjecthood such as part subject, part resistance and part reconciliation and use these formulations to argue that resistance to repression/oppression in both therapy and the Occupation could better be done by collaboration between the related sides. This allows mutual reinforcement of the resisting effort. I illustrate these ideas by vignettes from the Palestinian-Israeli arena.

Training analyst (DPG, DGPT). Numerous publications to epistemological, psychosomatic, socio-psychological, and psychoanalytical topics.

language, consciousness, the unconscious, Freud, Lorenzer

The author compares Freud’s and Lorenzer’s conceptualisations of the relationship between language, consciousness and the unconscious. Freud and Lorenzer are like-minded in grounding consciousness in the addition of words to representations, characterising unconscious representations as having lost the linguistic signs originally belonging to them, and in their view that these unconscious representations re-appear in consciousness under false names. Among other issues, however, in answering the questions of how linguistic signs and representations are linked with each other and why the unconscious representations re-appear in consciousness, they differ in their understandings of symbols. They also differ with regard to the relation between the biological and social nature of humankind.

The discourse of hysteria as the logic of mass consumption

Julio de Castro

Julio de Castro

Brazil

Julio de Castro   ajulio@jclcastro.com.br
mass consumption, advertising, discourse of hysteria, desire, enjoyment

The dynamics of mass consumption – from the 19th century, when its early developments took place, to the 1960s, when the transition to post-Fordist flexible consumption set in – articulate economic, social, and cultural factors. This article describes the mechanisms of mass consumption in terms of the algorithm of the discourse of hysteria, which for Lacan represents one of the fundamental kinds of social links. In this scheme, the consumer, driven by his lack, directs a question about his own desire to the advertiser, to the models used to seduce him, and to the targets that he, in turn, is encouraged to seduce. This interpellation results in a knowledge that attempts to deal with the consumer’s desire and projects itself on the universe of merchandise. Such a process simultaneously generates partial enjoyment and dissatisfaction, and both motivate it to repeat itself indefinitely.

This paper draws on psychoanalytic theories of embodiment to theorize the child’s creative use of objects and signs to represent a gendered sense of self. Turning to Winnicott’s concept of “true self,” we extend this symbolic labour to the transgender child to illustrate the psychic processes of embodiment that contribute to a meaningful gendered existence otherwise obstructed by social hatred and transphobia. transference, countertransference, Israel, Palestine, occupation, Zionism

The authors, a Palestinian psychiatrist working in the West Bank and a Jewish American child psychiatrist in New York, report on varieties of problematic transference and countertransference phenomena observed among mental health clinicians and patients across the Israeli/Palestinian divide. Reciprocal transference and countertransference anxieties were asymmetrical, reflecting the broader power relationship between Israelis and Palestinians. The Israeli clinicians’ need to regulate and to silence Palestinian “aggression”—either real or presumed—interfered with empathy, trust, genuine dialogue, and learning. The authors suggest that, to account for these findings, the psychoanalytic model of collective trauma must be integrated with motivational models from other disciplines in order to capture the roles played by social forces such as political propaganda, the silencing of social dissent, and longstanding historical agendas of military and economic domination.

Virtual Iraq/Afghanistan, a virtual reality (VR) exposure therapy designed for the treatment of combat-related PTSD, has generated wide public interest in the wake of growing concerns over mental health problems among service members. This paper offers a psychoanalytically informed reflection on how the environmental crisis has been framed and debated. The author draws attention to the ways in which apparently radical responses to the environmental crisis may often only reinforce established sociopolitical positions. Enactments of otherness and searching for a third space in the Palestine-Israel matrix

Lara Sheehi and Stephen Sheehi

Stephen Sheehi

USA

USA

Stephen Sheehi  

Palestine, Israel, enactment, third space, otherness, Buber

This article offers an exploration of the Third Space possibilities within the inter-subjective experience of Palestinians and Israelis. It explores the sociopolitical forces that constitute psychological threats to potential Third Spaces. We map the psychic structures that govern the relationship between Jewish Israelis and Palestinians, inside Israel and in the Occupied Territories. We will see how these relationships are fundamentally structured by asymmetries of power and subjectivity, resulting in closures of possibilities that could constitute a workable and genuinely reciprocal inter-subjective space of relatedness. As a result, their interaction is characterized by a series of what we term “enactments of otherness,” masterfully preemptive defensive processes that safeguard the object from further oppression and denigration. These enactments may arise from a “perverse” relationship between dominating and dominated subjects; however, they do not preclude the potential for creating radical alternative spaces and subjectivities from which Israelis and Palestinians can, together, co-create viable inter-subjectivities.

Given the overwhelming attention paid to the mother-child dyad in all realms of psychology and many in sociology, what theoretical frameworks are available to us through which to explore and understand father-daughter relationships? More specifically, what significance might working class fathers, both the flesh and blood person and the ‘father in the mind’ so frequently approached through the realm of the imaginary, have for their daughters’ relationship with education? Drawing on a longitudinal study of girls growing up from 4 to 21 years old, we look to the work of psychoanalytic and psychosocial theorists to think about the place of fathers in the educational experiences, trajectories and outcomes of working class girls and young women. In doing so, we want to disassemble some of the ‘heteronormative unconscious’ ideas and phantasies, so often dependent on splitting, that are attached to femininity and masculinity, especially in their classed representations. We also want to explore the ways in which the terms of gender are simultaneously fixed and fluid, binary and challenging of the binary, when we consider working class girls and young women’s relationships with their fathers and the connections that these may have with education and schooling.

Queer children and LGBT youth often continue to find in the psychotherapeutic setting and the clinical literature an ill-prepared and even aversive reception. Suicidality among such children draws especially sharp attention to the need for better alternatives to current treatment modalities—the focus here is chiefly on the relational area, with its emphasis on the coupling norm and attachment theory—and, more broadly, for the further comprehensive development of queer- and LGBT-affirmative psychoanalytic theory and practice. Neuroscience has become a popular source of metaphors and images for political and social theorists. Among the most popular is the “missing moment,” used to characterize the delay between an unconscious experience and the subject’s reaction. The goal, several authors suggest, is to come closer to the original non-conscious experience, wherein resides real freedom. If one follows this argument very far, however, it begins to look a lot like a popular theory of trauma. More troublingly, it leaves no room for either a psychoanalytic or narrative account that stresses the role of human relationships and human community in confronting trauma. In opposition to this account, this article sets the work of Stern, Segal, and Winnicott.

Eras of feminism differ in the programs, campaigns and critiques advanced, and in the sense of what is at stake. Taking up the identity of feminist has always meant weathering projections—attempts to induce shame, insults to one’s sexual identity, and attacks upon one’s femininity or basic adequacy as a woman. But feminist commitments also carry a range of moral and ethical dilemmas. This paper considers what psychoanalysis has to offer in working through conflicts that arise in feminist activism, focusing on three recurring dilemmas where struggles for recognition and moral authority carry ethical implications.

third-wave feminism, psychoanalysis, good/bad feminist, pleasure, adolescence, death drive

2014 saw a surge in discussions in the media and in feminist circles around who is a feminist and what it takes to be one: critics proclaimed that pop singer Beyoncé is not a feminist; Katy Perry and Lady Gaga reject the label; and Roxane Gay published a collection of essays, Bad Feminist (2014), on the topic. This paper works from and against the claim that third-wave feminism is rife with “undutiful daughters” and reads many of today’s feminists as “bad psychoanalysts” whose investment in reading desire often leads to a misreading. In positioning American pop sensation Lana Del Rey vis-à-vis Sophocles’ Antigone, I argue that these undutiful daughters ask us to interrogate what it means to make one’s desire ambiguously legible, and how that might work with, from, or against third-wave feminism. This paper contends that Del Rey and Antigone’s childlike attitudes, and their decision to remain undutiful daughters, offer a new model of willfulness that is integral to feminism today.
